title: Deal Acceleration: Tactical Battlecard vs LLM API Providers
summary: Tactical battlecard focused on accelerating mid-stage deals (POC -> Contract). Emphasis on technical objections (latency, cost, model regressions), commercial levers (pilot terms, reserved capacity), and demo/POC scripts sales engineers can run in 30–90 minutes.
content:
Purpose and scope:
This document is a compact, tactical battlecard to help AEs and SEs push stalled LLM API deals to close. Target situations: POC nearing completion, procurement asking for SLA/price concessions, or technical teams worried about latency and cost. Not exhaustive — use as a one-page reference in calls or deal rooms.

Top-level positioning to use on calls (30–60s):
- We’re an inference platform built for production economics: consistent latency, predictable unit cost, and operational controls (rollouts, fallback policies) that keep product UX stable as traffic scales.
- Quick anchor: "We can guarantee burst-ready throughput and a fallback model path so your app won’t degrade in spikes — that's the difference between prototype and product."

Competitor archetypes & sales cues (how opponents typically frame themselves):
- Lightweight Hosted APIs: pitch = "easy to start, low friction, single model stack." Cue: they avoid SLA/enterprise pricing. Trap: they lack dedicated capacity and observability for production loads.
- Commodity Cloud Endpoints / Managed Model Hosting: pitch = "you control models, we handle infra." Cue: emphasize customizability. Trap: ops and orchestration gap — customers still own complex scaling and cost tradeoffs.
- Open-stack/On-prem Inference Vendors: pitch = "full control, pay once." Cue: compliance and data control. Trap: heavy ops burden and slow iteration cycles.

Compact feature comparison (talking points — pick 3 for each demo):
- Latency: Redwood offers latency SLOs, continuous batching optimizations, and prefix caching. Competitors often report median latency but not tail percentiles or production SLOs.
- Cost predictability: Reserved pools + token-level breakdowns vs purely usage billing. Use reserved vs on-demand examples for customer sizing.
- Fallbacks & reliability: Automated fallback model routing and regional failover. Competitors either do manual fallback or none.
- Observability: token-level cost, per-request trace IDs, quality regressions tied to eval suites. Competitors rarely surface quality regression alerts.
- Deployment modes: Hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private (VPC/on-prem) from same control plane. Competitors typically force one pattern.

Common objections + concise rebuttals (script-ready):
- "Your price per token is higher than X."
  Rebuttal: "We see unit price as one input — the real metric is $/successful-session at target latency. With batching, caching, and reserved pools you often reduce overall cost by 20–50% versus raw per-token comparisons. We can run a 2-week traffic-matched pilot and share dollar-per-session math to prove it."
- "We can self-host with lower long-term costs."
  Rebuttal: "Self-host reduces single-unit cost but shifts engineering costs and risk. We provide predictable SLA-backed capacity, rollout tooling, and automated fallbacks — those save you incidents and engineering days. We'll run a TCO model for 12 months including SRE hours and incident probabilities."
- "Latency spikes are fine for us."
  Rebuttal: "Spikes correlate directly to dropout in user engagement. We can show customer A/B data where 40% of users dropped off at higher tail latency. Our routing+burst capacity guarantees reduce that tail exposure."
- "We need strict compliance (data residency, audit)."
  Rebuttal: "We offer Dedicated and Private deployments with KMS integrations, audit logs, and SOC/ISO docs. We can propose an exec-level legal/infra workshop to map controls to their policies."

Technical traps to call out on discovery (questions to ask the customer):
- How do you measure tail latency today (p95/p99)? Can you share request size distribution?
- Do you have traffic patterns with large cold-start bursts (e.g., marketing campaigns, product launches)?
- How do you currently validate model quality changes in production? Any automated regression alerts?
- Who owns SLA remediation and what’s the cost of degraded UX for your product?

POC → Contract acceleration levers (commercial & technical):
- Offer a timeboxed pilot with defined success metrics: p95 latency target, $/session ceiling, and quality threshold (eval pass rate).
- Provide a limited reserved capacity pilot (discounted) to demonstrate stable tail latency.
- Commit to a rollback/fallback playbook and jointly authored runbook for cutover.
- Propose a mid-pilot business review at week 2 with cost and latency dashboards and a clear decision gate.

Demo and SE playbook (30–90 minute run):
1) Prep (15m): Load a representative sample traffic file (use their sample or our synthetic generator), ensure API keys and selected models are configured.
2) Baseline run (15m): Run traffic against an on-demand instance and capture p50/p95/p99, token cost, and error rates.
3) Optimized run (20–30m): Flip to reserved pool + prefix caching + recommended batching config; show improvements in p95 and cost.
4) Failure injection (10m): Simulate node failure and show automated fallback to a lighter model variant and no user-visible errors.
5) Walkthrough (10m): Show cost-by-route, trace IDs, and quality regression alerts with sample prompt set.

Evidence and win themes to surface:
- Metric proof: before/after p95 reductions, token savings from caching, and dollars-per-session improvements.
- Playbook proof: documented rollback and canary policies used in existing customers.
- Support proof: SLA and escalation paths, named SE support during pilot.

Decision-stage scripts for procurement and legal: 
- Procurement: "We can harmonize pricing into a committed-reserved model with quarterly usage true-ups; pilot discounts will convert to initial committed volume with a 90-day review clause."
- Legal: "List of compliance artifacts we can provide immediately: SOC2 type II summary, encryption at rest/in transit docs, data processing addendum. For private deployments we have a standard VPC deployment checklist."

Red flags to escalate to AE manager or solutions architect: 
- Customer unable to provide request/size distribution (we need it to size pools).
- Security team requires an unscoped rewrite of our control plane for pilot.
- Customer insists on comparing per-token retail price without providing realistic traffic patterns.

Collateral & assets to attach to deal room:
- Short one-pager: pilot success metric template (use for the kickoff).
- Benchmark snapshots: p95/p99 before-after for similar customers.
- SE runbook: step-by-step demo script and failure injection commands.
- Pricing TCO template: 12-month TCO with SRE hours, incident costs, and unit pricing.

Success metrics to commit to with the customer (examples):
- p95 latency <= their target (e.g., 300ms for inference endpoint) during pilot window
- Token cost per successful session reduced by >= 10% vs baseline
- Quality eval pass rate >= 95% on the agreed prompt set

Quick checklist for AE/SE before closing: 
- Confirm we have traffic sample and expected QPS distribution
- Confirm legal/compliance artefact list and timeline
- Set pilot gate metrics and schedule week-2 review
- Load sample traffic and validate dashboards accessible to customer
- Prepare reserved pool sizing and discount proposal

Notes and tactics learned from recent wins (playbook refinements):
- Offering a short dedicated-reserved window (3–6 weeks) has closed pilot-to-contract 2x faster than on-demand pilots.
- Always show tail latency (p99) charts — median-only conversations rarely scale into contracts.
- Bring a pre-made rollback/runbook into the kickoff; customers appreciate operational thoughtfulness and it reduces risk conversations.

Appendix: rapid rebuttal snippets (copy/paste):
- "We’ll measure $/session — not raw token price — and aim to beat your current metric under load in a timeboxed pilot."
- "If security is a blocker, let’s scope a Private deployment workshop. It’s often a legal checkbox more than an engineering one."
- "We’ll put a named SE and a weekly cadence on the pilot — transparent metrics or you don’t pay beyond pilot terms."

End of battlecard. Keep this doc updated with new pilot outcomes and fresh benchmark charts.
